newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada dlr breaks through support, closes weaker.
newsitem.headline: Canada dlr breaks through support, closes weaker.

text.p: * Canada's dollar weakened to close at C$1.3930 (US$0.7178) in heavy trading on Wednesday after the currency broke through technical support at the C$1.3885 (US$0.7202) level, triggering a flurry of stop-loss orders, traders said. * They said comments by Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen failed to shield the Canada dollar against a strong market bias to sell.

"The stops were triggered and that was followed by some options activity at C$1.3900 (US$0.7194) which brought more (U.S.) dollar buyers into the market," said Reid Farrill, corporate foreign exchange adviser for CIBC Wood Gundy.
The Canada dollar sell-off added to a month-long downward trend that has lopped 2 percent off the currency's value against the U.S. dollar.
Some analysts said that additional comments by Thiessen concerning interest rate policy might have given a market pre-disposed to sell the Canada dollar a reason to follow through.

When asked how another U.S. rate hike would affect the Bank of Canada, Thiessen said a U.S. move would always have an impact. But Thiessen said an improved fiscal position helped provide the central bank with more flexibility.
"Thiessen repeated what he's repeated before, that the Bank of Canada does not have to follow the Fed," said Michael Gregory, economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers.

"Given that the market was already in a weakened state, technical pressures were building and there were rumors of a large knock-out option at C$1.3900 (US$0.7194), the market said, 'Sell,'" Gregory said.
The dollar sell-off surprised some economists who had speculated that the currency would rally after the release of U.S. economic data on Tuesday showing few inflationary pressures on the horizon.

U.S. consumer prices grew by 0.1 percent in May, below a Reuters forecast of a 0.2 percent rise, which added to a growing consensus that the Federal Reserve would not raise interest rates at the next FOMC meeting on July 1-2.
"It should have been more supportive of the Canadian dollar," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist with Bank of Montreal.
"We didn't see a Fed move in May, and with this recent data out yesterday, it doesn't look like we'll see one in July. Even a probability of a move in August is diminishing," Ferley said.
On the crosses, the Canada dollar dipped to 81.46 yen from Tuesday's 81.73 and to 1.2434 marks from Tuesday's 1.2480 marks.
